title: Wildfire smoke can turn intermittent school disruption into maternal employment loss
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35264, Where There's Smoke: Stochastic Caregiving Shocks and Mothers' Labor Market Outcomes
geography: United States; mothers and children exposed to wildfire smoke, school closures, and student absenteeism

observations.period: 2026 working paper; U.S. wildfire-smoke and school-disruption episodes studied over the source's administrative and survey-linked windows

denominator.unit: study-defined mother/child exposure sample; exact public abstract sample count not disclosed in this record

caregiving_shock.value: wildfire smoke increased school closures and student absenteeism, generating intermittent caregiving demand even where formal childcare was available

contemporaneous_cost.value: the smoke-linked caregiving shocks imposed substantial contemporaneous labor-market costs on mothers

accumulated_effect.value: when caregiving shocks accumulated, maternal employment declined
accumulated_effect.unit: employment response to repeated or accumulated shocks

workplace_tolerance_boundary.value: employment losses were fully offset among mothers working outside male-dominated industries, consistent with workplace tolerance moderating the consequence of intermittent caregiving demand
workplace_tolerance_boundary.unit: heterogeneous employment response by industry gender composition

downstream_outcome.value: the public abstract does not establish household income, paid or unpaid hours, schedule control, childcare substitution, health, housing, trust, or later employment recovery
downstream_outcome.unit: missing continuation of the care-to-room chain

observations.method: The paper uses plausibly exogenous variation in wildfire smoke exposure, links smoke to school closures and student absenteeism, and compares mothers whose youngest children differ in reliance on school-based childcare. It estimates contemporaneous and accumulated labor-market responses and heterogeneity by industry gender composition.
observations.uncertainty: The public NBER abstract does not disclose every sample restriction, exposure window, coefficient, or administrative linkage in this record. Smoke exposure is a quasi-experimental source of variation, but the result is not a complete household episode. Industry gender composition is a proxy for workplace tolerance, not a direct measure of employer policy, schedule control, or worker bargaining power.
observations.subgroup: Mothers differentiated by the youngest child's reliance on school-based childcare and by whether they work in male-dominated industries; wildfire-smoke exposure and school-disruption context vary by place and episode.
observations.counterinterpretation: Mothers in industries outside the male-dominated group may differ in occupation, schedule, remote-work access, pay, benefits, or local labor markets; the offset pattern does not prove that tolerance alone caused resilience. Formal childcare availability does not mean it can replace school-based care during smoke-related disruption.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for Working Paper 35264

boundary: This record adds a quasi-experimental material/time/care bridge: an environmental shock can intermittently remove a school-based care input, impose maternal labor-market costs, and produce accumulated employment loss, with an industry-level workplace-tolerance boundary. It does not establish a national employment effect, a household income or health path, or that male-dominated industries are the sole mechanism.
